item.title: ADR: Dev host: Fedora Server with Cockpit, Podman Quadlets and KVM
item.description: Context ADR 0002 chose Fedora Server with rootful Docker and a containerized Komodo Periphery as the baremetal Docker host, and assumed Proxmox for the dev machine. Since then: The dev machine (devbox) dropped Proxmox. It runs Fedora Server directly. Dev work focuses on infrastructure (VMs, cluster tooling) more than on long-running containers. Komodo’s Podman support is still rough (issue #504), but dev containers no longer need to be Komodo-managed. Decision devbox runs Fedora Server on bare metal. Management plane is Cockpit. KVM/libvirt hosts dev VMs, created with Terraform (libvirt provider) and managed in Cockpit. fedora-dev and other dev VMs are guests, not the host. Podman is the container runtime on the host. Host-level services run as Quadlets (systemd units) deployed by Ansible. If Quadlets prove awkward, podman-compose is an acceptable fallback. Komodo does not manage devbox itself. Komodo manages containers only on meadowprod (Debian prod) and on a Docker Test VM hosted on devbox, which runs Docker with Periphery. Other dev VMs are unmanaged by Komodo. Host provisioning and updates are run from Semaphore on nuclet. Consequences Positive

item.title: ADR: Organize infrastructure by purpose, not environment
item.description: Context The earlier model had Dev, Test and Prod environments, each Komodo-managed on Fedora + Docker, with a ResourceSync per environment following its own branch (ADR 0001). The hardware changed: UnRAID-to-TrueNAS migration was cancelled, Proxmox and Synology are gone, and Test/Lab became two clusters. There is no real promotion pipeline between machines.

item.title: ADR: Tailnet-per-environment (Prod / Test / Dev) with declarative node sharing
item.description: Status Rejected. The homelab will not split Prod/Test/Dev into separate tailnets. Environment separation stays as it is today: a single tailnet with tag-based grants. The investigation is retained in full because the rejection is the useful part — it documents why an appealing structural-isolation story doesn’t survive contact with an already-working Services deployment.

item.title: ADR: Workload isolation in a single tailnet — access pools
item.description: Status Proposed. Direction settled: workload/dev traffic stays in the current tailnet, separated by ACLs organized as access pools. The separate-tailnet option is deferred to a named trigger, not discarded. Extends ADR-0006, which rejected splitting Prod/Test/Dev into separate tailnets. That investigation’s useful finding was that the boundary axis was wrong, not the boundary idea. This ADR takes the next step of that finding: separation of workload from homelab is real, but the mechanism is pools within one boundary, with structural separation preserved as an off-ramp.

item.title: ADR: Orchestration Model — Docker-native vs Kubernetes/ArgoCD for the Homelab
item.description: Context The homelab currently standardizes on Docker (rootful, on Fedora Server baremetal hosts) managed through Komodo for GitOps. The prior narrative decision (“Komodo over Kubernetes (K3s + ArgoCD)” in planning/decisions.md) chose Docker-native Komodo over a K3s + ArgoCD stack on the grounds of complexity, risk tolerance, and concept alignment with existing familiarity with compose files.

item.title: ADR: Skip local Docker registry, focus on git pipeline
item.description: Context The homelab needs a strategy for managing container images between the local environment and production. Initial considerations included running a local container registry (Artifactory/Lightwell analog) or relying on Docker Hub with version pinning. The homelab already uses Komodo GitOps, GitHub Actions for rendering, and Ansible validation playbooks. Goals: Avoid infrastructure overhead — A local registry adds a running service, storage management, and maintenance burden for a feature (offline access) that isn’t actually required. Leverage existing pipeline investment — GitHub Actions, Ansible validation, and Komodo ResourceSync are already in place and can be extended to cover image governance. Security evaluation through PR process — Image scanning and review can happen in Git before anything gets deployed, rather than after images sit in a registry. Version pinning is already the pattern — Komodo configs and Git branches already provide effective version control; a registry would be redundant. Decision Skip running a local Docker registry as a stop-gap. Instead:

item.title: ADR: Container Runtime Tradeoffs — Docker (Rootful), Docker (Rootless), and Podman
item.description: Context Selecting a container runtime for baremetal Docker hosts involves balancing security, operational convenience, and tooling compatibility. This ADR breaks down three approaches and the fundamental tension between central-socket management and daemonless isolation. The host OS decision is handled in ADR 0002: Baremetal Docker Host OS Selection. Runtime Options Docker (Rootful) The classic model: dockerd runs as root, exposes /var/run/docker.sock.

item.title: ADR: Per-environment Git branches via Komodo ResourceSync
item.description: Superseded by ADR 0009. Environments are no longer the organizing axis; a single ResourceSync follows main. Kept below for history. Context The homelab uses Komodo with ResourceSync to declare servers, stacks, deployments, and related resources from Git (an “app-of-apps” style flow: Git remains the audit trail; Komodo reconciles). Goals: main shows the whole picture — dev/, test/, and prod/ (or equivalent komodo/{dev,test,prod}/) layouts exist together on main so reviews and long-lived docs match reality after merges. Per-environment steering — each environment’s sync can follow main or follow a named branch (for example to soak a stack change in Dev before it lands on main). Homelab-realistic ergonomics — accept some manual merge hygiene instead of building full release automation up front. An earlier sketch of this approach lived in wip/komodo-artifact-templates/scratch/branch_management_ideas.md.
